summary.text: Split into the four residue classes modulo \(4\), using the explicit distinct-part witnesses \(\{n\}\), \(\{9,n-9\}\), \(\{18,n-18\}\), and \(\{27,n-27\}\), with the last replaced by \(\{27\}\) when \(n=27\).  The fixed parts are divisible by \(9=3^2\), while each remaining part is divisible by \(4=2^2\), so all parts are nonsquarefree; the bound and congruences ensure the parts are positive and distinct.

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)\) denote the number of partitions of \(n\) into distinct positive nonsquarefree parts. More precisely, let
\[
S_n=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.
\]
Then \(a(n)\) is the cardinality of the collection of finite subsets \(P\subseteq S_n\) such that
\[
\sum_{k\in P}k=n
\]
and every \(k\in P\) is nonsquarefree. Because \(P\) is a set rather than a multiset, its elements are automatically distinct.

We first record the elementary criterion that will establish that all the parts used below are nonsquarefree. A positive integer is squarefree only if it is not divisible by the square of any prime. Consequently:

* if \(4\mid k\), then \(2^2\mid k\), so \(k\) is not squarefree;
* if \(9\mid k\), then \(3^2\mid k\), so \(k\) is not squarefree.

We will also use the following direct consequence of the definition of \(a(n)\). If we exhibit a finite set \(P\) such that every member of \(P\) is positive and at most \(n\), the members are nonsquarefree, and their sum is \(n\), then \(P\subseteq S_n\) is one of the subsets counted by \(a(n)\). Thus the counted collection is nonempty, so its cardinality satisfies \(a(n)\ge 1\), and hence \(a(n)>0\).

Now fix an integer \(n>23\). Thus \(n\ge 24\). We split into the four possible residue classes of \(n\) modulo \(4\).

**Case 1: \(n\equiv 0\pmod 4\).**

Take
\[
P=\{n\}.
\]
Its only part is positive, is at most \(n\), and is divisible by \(4\), hence is nonsquarefree. The sum of the elements of \(P\) is plainly \(n\). Therefore this is an admissible partition, and \(a(n)>0\).

**Case 2: \(n\equiv 1\pmod 4\).**

Since \(n>23\) and has residue \(1\) modulo \(4\), we have \(n\ge 25\). Take
\[
P=\{9,n-9\}.
\]
Both parts are positive: \(9>0\), while \(n-9\ge 16>0\). They are also at most \(n\). The first part, \(9\), is divisible by \(9\), so it is nonsquarefree. Moreover, since both \(n\) and \(9\) are congruent to \(1\) modulo \(4\),
\[
n-9\equiv 1-1\equiv 0\pmod 4.
\]
Thus \(4\mid(n-9)\), and the second part is nonsquarefree as well.

The two parts are distinct. Indeed, if \(9=n-9\), then \(n=18\), contradicting \(n\ge25\). Finally,
\[
9+(n-9)=n.
\]
Hence \(P\) is an admissible partition of \(n\) into distinct nonsquarefree parts, and \(a(n)>0\).

**Case 3: \(n\equiv 2\pmod 4\).**

Here \(n>23\) implies \(n\ge26\). Take
\[
P=\{18,n-18\}.
\]
The first part is positive, and the second satisfies \(n-18\ge8>0\); both are at most \(n\). Since \(9\mid18\), the part \(18\) is nonsquarefree. Also \(18\equiv2\pmod4\), so
\[
n-18\equiv2-2\equiv0\pmod4.
\]
Therefore \(4\mid(n-18)\), and this second part is nonsquarefree.

These two parts are distinct. For if \(18=n-18\), then \(n=36\), but \(36\equiv0\pmod4\), contrary to the present assumption that \(n\equiv2\pmod4\). Their sum is
\[
18+(n-18)=n.
\]
Thus they form an admissible partition, proving \(a(n)>0\) in this case.

**Case 4: \(n\equiv 3\pmod 4\).**

The least integer greater than \(23\) with residue \(3\) modulo \(4\) is \(27\). We first handle this boundary value separately.

If \(n=27\), take
\[
P=\{27\}.
\]
The part \(27\) is positive, is at most \(n\), and is divisible by \(9\), so it is nonsquarefree. Its sum is \(27=n\), giving an admissible partition and hence \(a(27)>0\).

Now suppose \(n\ne27\). Since the integers congruent to \(3\) modulo \(4\) occur four apart, the assumptions \(n>23\), \(n\equiv3\pmod4\), and \(n\ne27\) imply \(n\ge31\). Take
\[
P=\{27,n-27\}.
\]
The first part is positive, while \(n-27\ge4>0\), and both parts are at most \(n\). Because \(9\mid27\), the first part is nonsquarefree. Furthermore, \(27\equiv3\pmod4\), and hence
\[
n-27\equiv3-3\equiv0\pmod4.
\]
Thus the second part is divisible by \(4\) and is also nonsquarefree.

The parts are distinct. If \(27=n-27\), then \(n=54\); however, \(54\equiv2\pmod4\), contradicting \(n\equiv3\pmod4\). Finally,
\[
27+(n-27)=n.
\]
So this too is an admissible partition, and \(a(n)>0\).

The four cases exhaust all possible residues of \(n\) modulo \(4\). Therefore, for every integer \(n>23\), there exists at least one partition of \(n\) into distinct nonsquarefree parts. Consequently,
\[
\boxed{a(n)>0\quad\text{for every }n>23.}
\]
